Voyager mission timeline

23 key moments from 1977 to today. Open any event to see what happened, the context around it, why it matters and where the information comes from. Where helpful, the spacecraft’s distance from the Sun on that date is shown from JPL Horizons data.

23 / 23
  1. August 20, 1977 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 launches
    What happened
    A Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket lifts Voyager 2 off from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
    Context
    It launches first but on the slower of the two trajectories — the one that keeps Uranus and Neptune within reach.
    Why it matters
    The launch window used a planetary alignment that recurs only about every 175 years.
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 2
  2. September 5, 1977 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 launches
    What happened
    Voyager 1 lifts off 16 days after its twin, on a faster, shorter path to Jupiter.
    Context
    Because it will arrive first, it is named Voyager 1. It overtakes Voyager 2 in distance from the Sun before the end of 1977.
    Why it matters
    Its faster route is why it is still the most distant spacecraft today.
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  3. March 5, 1979 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 at Jupiter
    What happened
    Closest approach to Jupiter. Images reveal erupting volcanoes on the moon Io and a faint ring around the planet.
    Context
    Jupiter’s gravity raises the probe’s speed from about 14 to about 23 km/s relative to the Sun (JPL Horizons data).
    Why it matters
    Io was the first place beyond Earth seen to be volcanically active, showing that tidal heating can keep small worlds geologically alive.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 5.3 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  4. July 9, 1979 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 at Jupiter
    What happened
    Voyager 2 flies past Jupiter four months after its twin, getting better views of the moon Europa and watching how Io’s volcanoes had changed.
    Context
    Having two flybys months apart let scientists see a changing system rather than a single snapshot.
    Why it matters
    Europa’s cracked, young-looking ice surface was an early hint of the ocean now thought to lie beneath it.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 5.3 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 2
  5. November 12, 1980 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 at Saturn and Titan
    What happened
    Voyager 1 passes Saturn and makes a close flyby of its largest moon, Titan, finding a thick nitrogen atmosphere hidden under orange haze.
    Context
    The Titan pass bends Voyager 1 out of the planets’ plane, ending its planetary tour.
    Why it matters
    A deliberate trade-off: scientists valued Titan over later planets — and Titan later became the target of the Huygens probe.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 9.5 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  6. August 25, 1981 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 at Saturn
    What happened
    Voyager 2 studies Saturn’s rings and atmosphere; its route is chosen to keep Uranus reachable.
    Context
    A jammed camera platform briefly interrupted observations after closest approach; engineers later worked around it.
    Why it matters
    Saturn’s gravity assist set up the only visits ever made to Uranus and Neptune.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 9.6 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 2
  7. January 24, 1986 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 at Uranus
    What happened
    The first and only close flyby of Uranus: ten new moons, two new rings and a magnetic field tilted about 60° from the rotation axis.
    Context
    Engineers had reprogrammed the spacecraft on the way so it could return data from much farther away.
    Why it matters
    Nearly everything we know about Uranus up close still comes from these few days.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 19.1 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 2
  8. August 25, 1989 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 at Neptune and Triton
    What happened
    Voyager 2 finds the Great Dark Spot storm, the fastest winds measured on any planet, complete but faint rings, and plumes erupting on the moon Triton.
    Context
    The encounter bends Voyager 2 south of the planets’ plane and slows it slightly relative to the Sun.
    Why it matters
    It completed the reconnaissance of all four giant planets — 12 years after launch.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 30.2 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 2
  9. January 1, 1990 · Both spacecraftThe Voyager Interstellar Mission begins
    What happened
    NASA formally extends the mission with a new goal: to explore the outer heliosphere and reach interstellar space.
    Context
    Cameras and planetary instruments were no longer needed; fields-and-particles instruments became the focus.
    Why it matters
    It turned a planetary mission into a 35-year-plus journey to the edge of the Sun’s influence.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 39.9 AU (Voyager 1) · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager mission
  10. February 14, 1990 · Voyager 1Family portrait and the Pale Blue Dot
    What happened
    Voyager 1 photographs six planets from about 40 AU, including Earth as a speck smaller than a pixel.
    Context
    These were the last images either Voyager would take; the cameras were switched off soon afterwards.
    Why it matters
    It became one of the most recognised images in science and a lasting symbol of Earth’s fragility.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 40.4 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1’s Pale Blue Dot
  11. February 17, 1998 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 becomes the most distant human-made object
    What happened
    At about 69 AU, Voyager 1 overtakes Pioneer 10.
    Context
    Pioneer 10 launched five years earlier but was slower; Voyager 1 has held the record ever since.
    Why it matters
    Every distance on this site’s tracker is, literally, a new human record being set in real time.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 69.4 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  12. December 16, 2004 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 crosses the termination shock
    What happened
    At about 94 AU the solar wind around Voyager 1 abruptly slows from supersonic to subsonic speed.
    Context
    This marks entry into the heliosheath, the turbulent outer layer of the heliosphere.
    Why it matters
    It was the first direct detection of the heliosphere’s inner boundary.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 94 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  13. August 30, 2007 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 crosses the termination shock
    What happened
    Voyager 2 reaches the termination shock at about 84 AU — roughly 10 AU closer to the Sun than Voyager 1 did.
    Context
    Its working plasma instrument measured the crossing directly — several times, as the shock moved back and forth.
    Why it matters
    The different distances showed the heliosphere is asymmetric, pushed in on one side.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 83.7 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 2
  14. August 25, 2012 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 enters interstellar space
    What happened
    At about 121.6 AU, particles from the Sun drop sharply and galactic cosmic rays rise.
    Context
    Because its plasma instrument had failed, confirmation came only in 2013, when solar-storm-driven plasma waves revealed much denser surrounding gas.
    Why it matters
    The first human-made object to leave the Sun’s protective bubble.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 121.6 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  15. November 28, 2017 · Voyager 1Thrusters fired after 37 years
    What happened
    Engineers test Voyager 1’s trajectory-correction thrusters, unused since 1980, and use them for attitude control.
    Context
    The attitude thrusters in use had degraded; the old set still worked after decades of cold.
    Why it matters
    It extended the mission by keeping the antenna pointed at Earth.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 140.4 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA Science — Voyager 1
  16. November 5, 2018 · Voyager 2Voyager 2 enters interstellar space
    What happened
    At about 119 AU its plasma instrument sees the solar wind stop — a direct measurement of the heliopause.
    Context
    NASA announced the crossing in December 2018, after the data had been analysed.
    Why it matters
    A second crossing, in a different direction, turned one data point into a comparison.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 119 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Voyager 2 enters interstellar space
  17. June 13, 2024 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 recovers from a memory fault
    What happened
    After sending unreadable data since November 2023, Voyager 1 again returns science from all four instruments then operating.
    Context
    A failed chip had corrupted part of the flight data system’s memory; engineers moved the affected code elsewhere.
    Why it matters
    A software repair made from more than 24 billion km away, with a two-day command-and-reply cycle.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 163.7 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Voyager 1 returning science data from all four instruments
  18. October 1, 2024 · Voyager 2Voyager 2’s plasma instrument switched off
    What happened
    NASA turns off Voyager 2’s plasma science instrument to save power.
    Context
    The instrument had returned little data recently because of its orientation relative to the plasma flow.
    Why it matters
    Part of a long-planned sequence to keep the spacecraft operating as power declines.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 137.7 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Turns off science instrument to save Voyager 2 power
  19. February 25, 2025 · Both spacecraftTwo more instruments switched off
    What happened
    Voyager 1’s cosmic ray subsystem is turned off on 25 February; Voyager 2’s low-energy charged particle instrument follows on 24 March.
    Context
    NASA said that without these steps the probes might have had only months of power left.
    Why it matters
    Trading some science for time keeps both spacecraft returning data for longer.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 166.2 AU (Voyager 1) · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Turns off 2 Voyager science instruments
  20. March 20, 2025 · Voyager 1Voyager 1’s primary roll thrusters revived
    What happened
    Thrusters out of use since their heaters lost power in 2004 are brought back as a fallback.
    Context
    The backup thrusters then in use were at risk of clogging; engineers suspected a switch had been flipped, and were right.
    Why it matters
    Losing attitude control would mean losing contact; this bought a margin of safety.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 166.5 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Voyager 1 revives backup thrusters before command pause
  21. April 17, 2026 · Voyager 1Voyager 1’s LECP switched off
    What happened
    The low-energy charged particle instrument, operating almost continuously since 1977, is turned off.
    Context
    A small motor that rotates the sensor was left on, which could allow the instrument to be revived later.
    Why it matters
    Voyager 1 is left with its magnetometer and plasma wave instrument.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 170.3 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Shuts off instrument on Voyager 1
  22. August 4, 2026 · Voyager 2Power-saving swap extends Voyager 2
    What happened
    NASA reports that engineers replaced several power-hungry devices on Voyager 2 with lower-power alternatives in one coordinated change.
    Context
    The same change is planned for Voyager 1 in the following months.
    Why it matters
    It keeps Voyager 2’s three remaining instruments running for at least another year.
    Distance from Sun
    ≈ 143.6 AU · JPL Horizons
    Source
    NASA — Engineers help prolong Voyager 2’s science mission
  23. November 18, 2026 · Voyager 1Voyager 1 one light-day from Earth (upcoming)
    What happened
    NASA projects that Voyager 1 will be about 25.9 billion km from Earth — the distance light travels in 24 hours.
    Context
    This site’s model independently puts the crossing on the same date.
    Why it matters
    No human-made object has ever been a full light-day away.
    Source
    NASA — Where are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 now?

About these dates

Encounter dates are closest-approach dates in UTC. Interstellar crossings are dates later identified in the data, not the dates they were announced. Descriptions are written by this site from the linked NASA/JPL material. Distances are interpolated from monthly JPL samples and are approximate around flybys. See these events on the distance chart.
